questions.question: What is AWS Elastic Beanstalk and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: AWS Elastic Beanstalk is a Platform as a Service (PaaS) that automatically handles deployment, capacity provisioning, load balancing, auto-scaling, and health monitoring of web applications. It solves the problem of infrastructure complexity — without it, developers must manually provision EC2, configure load balancers, set up auto scaling, and manage monitoring for every application they deploy.

questions.question: What is the difference between an Application and an Environment in Elastic Beanstalk?
questions.answer: An Application is a logical container that holds all versions of your code and all environments. Think of it like a GitHub repository. An Environment is the actual running deployment — it contains real AWS resources like EC2 instances, security groups, and load balancers. One Application can have multiple Environments (e.g., Dev, Test, Production) running simultaneously and independently.

questions.question: Is Elastic Beanstalk free to use?
questions.answer: Yes — Elastic Beanstalk itself has no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying AWS resources it provisions, such as EC2 instances, EBS storage, RDS databases, and Elastic Load Balancers. A single-instance environment with a free-tier eligible EC2 type (t2.micro or t3.micro) and 10 GB EBS storage falls within the AWS Free Tier for the first 12 months.

questions.question: Which AWS infrastructure-as-code service does Elastic Beanstalk use internally?
questions.answer: Elastic Beanstalk uses AWS CloudFormation internally. When you create an environment, Beanstalk creates a CloudFormation stack containing all the provisioned resources. You can see this stack in the CloudFormation console. You should never manually delete this stack — always terminate environments through the Elastic Beanstalk console to ensure proper, ordered cleanup.

questions.question: What programming languages and platforms does Elastic Beanstalk support?
questions.answer: Elastic Beanstalk supports: Java (on Tomcat), Python, .NET (on Windows Server), Node.js, PHP, Ruby, Go, and Docker (including multi-container Docker). This covers the majority of web application stacks. For unsupported runtimes, you can use Docker to containerize the application and deploy it on Beanstalk.

questions.question: What health status colors does Elastic Beanstalk use and what does each mean?
questions.answer: Elastic Beanstalk uses four health status colors: Green (Ok — all resources functioning correctly), Yellow (Warning — some health checks failing, investigation required), Red (Degraded/Severe — application unavailable or critical errors), and Grey (Pending/No data — environment is launching or health data not yet available). A new environment starts Grey and transitions to Green once fully deployed.

questions.question: What two environment types does Elastic Beanstalk support and when would you use each?
questions.answer: Elastic Beanstalk supports Web Server environments and Worker environments. Web Server environments handle incoming HTTP/HTTPS requests — used for websites and REST APIs. Worker environments process background tasks pulled from an Amazon SQS queue — used for long-running or asynchronous workloads like video transcoding, email sending, or data processing pipelines.

questions.question: What AWS resources does Elastic Beanstalk create for a typical single-instance web application?
questions.answer: For a single-instance environment, Elastic Beanstalk creates: an EC2 instance (running your application), a Security Group (controlling traffic), an Elastic IP address (static public IP for EC2), an S3 bucket (storing code versions and logs), and CloudWatch metrics (monitoring CPU, requests, latency). It does NOT create an ELB or Auto Scaling Group for single-instance environments.

questions.question: Why should you choose Single Instance over Load Balanced when learning Elastic Beanstalk?
questions.answer: A Load Balanced environment automatically creates an Elastic Load Balancer, which costs approximately $0.008 per hour (around $5.76/month) and is NOT free tier eligible. Charges begin immediately upon environment creation. A Single Instance environment uses only a free-tier eligible EC2 instance with no ELB. For learning and testing, Single Instance is always the right choice to avoid unexpected charges.

questions.question: What happens to S3 buckets when you terminate an Elastic Beanstalk environment?
questions.answer: S3 buckets created by Elastic Beanstalk are NOT automatically deleted when you terminate an environment. The code versions and logs stored in S3 persist. You must manually empty and delete the S3 bucket (typically named elasticbeanstalk-[region]-[account-id]) after terminating your environment to avoid ongoing storage charges. This is one of the most common sources of unexpected billing for beginners.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to deploy an application quickly with minimal setup. How did you approach it?
questions.answer: (Situation) I needed to deploy a Java web application for a team demo within an hour but had limited infrastructure setup time. (Task) Get the application live on AWS with a public URL and basic monitoring without manual EC2 configuration. (Action) I used Elastic Beanstalk — uploaded the WAR file, selected Java on Amazon Linux 2, configured a single-instance environment with the Default VPC and Public IP enabled, and submitted. (Result) Within 5 minutes the environment was Green and the application was live at the Beanstalk domain URL. Total setup time was under 10 minutes compared to the 45+ minutes manual EC2 configuration would have required.

questions.question: Describe how you would set up a safe deployment workflow for a production web application on Elastic Beanstalk.
questions.answer: (Situation) A production Elastic Beanstalk application serving real users needed a safe update process. (Task) Deploy new features without downtime and with instant rollback capability. (Action) I implemented a multi-environment strategy: one environment for Dev (All at Once — fast, downtime acceptable), one for Staging (Rolling — validates the deployment), and Production using Immutable deployment (new instances created, health-checked, then old instances terminated). For critical releases I used Blue/Green — deployed to a Green environment, tested thoroughly, then swapped CNAMEs. (Result) Zero-downtime deployments with rollback achievable in under 60 seconds by swapping CNAMEs back.

questions.question: A colleague tells you that after terminating their Elastic Beanstalk environment their AWS bill still shows charges. How would you diagnose and fix this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Unexpected charges after environment termination. (Task) Identify the remaining billable resources. (Action) I would check: (1) S3 — Beanstalk S3 buckets with stored code versions and logs persist after termination. Empty and delete the bucket. (2) RDS — if the environment included an integrated RDS instance, check whether it was retained instead of deleted. (3) CloudFormation — if the stack is in DELETE_FAILED state, manually retry deletion after clearing blocking resources. (4) Elastic IPs — unattached EIPs incur charges. (Result) Identified and deleted the S3 bucket with 2 GB of old logs, eliminating all ongoing charges.

questions.question: Your Elastic Beanstalk environment health turns Yellow during peak business hours. What steps would you take?
questions.answer: (Situation) Production Elastic Beanstalk environment health degraded to Yellow during peak traffic. (Task) Identify and resolve the issue before it turns Red. (Action) First, check the Events tab for recent Beanstalk events indicating what changed. Then go to Monitoring tab and check CPU Utilization, 5xx error rate, and request latency — a spike in any of these typically explains Yellow health. If CPU is high, consider scaling up instance type or enabling Auto Scaling. If 5xx errors are high, check application logs via Logs tab. (Result) Found CPU at 92% on a single t3.micro — upgraded to t3.small and environment returned to Green within 2 minutes.

questions.question: A testing team needs their own copy of the production application to run QA tests without affecting live users. How would you set this up in Elastic Beanstalk?
questions.answer: (Situation) QA team needs a dedicated testing environment that mirrors production. (Task) Provide an independent environment in the same application where testers can deploy code and run tests freely. (Action) In the existing Elastic Beanstalk application, I created a second environment named MyApp-Test as a single-instance environment (to keep costs low). Deployed the same application version to it. The QA team received the separate URL for their environment. Any changes they make — deployments, configuration changes — are completely isolated from the Production environment. (Result) QA team had a full working environment within 10 minutes. Three subsequent deployments to Test never affected production.

questions.question: How would you securely pass database credentials to an application running on Elastic Beanstalk?
questions.answer: (Situation) A web application on Beanstalk needs to connect to an RDS database securely. (Task) Pass DB credentials without hard-coding them in source code. (Action) Use Elastic Beanstalk Environment Variables — in the Beanstalk console go to Configuration → Software → Environment Properties and add DB_HOST, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD. The application reads these at runtime via environment variable access (e.g., os.environ in Python). For production, I would additionally use AWS Secrets Manager — store the credentials there and have the application retrieve them via the Secrets Manager API, rotating credentials automatically. (Result) Credentials never appear in source code, version control, or deployment packages.

questions.question: Explain the difference between All at Once, Rolling, and Immutable deployments and when to use each.
questions.answer: (Situation) Choosing the right Elastic Beanstalk deployment strategy for different environments. (Task) Match deployment strategy to risk tolerance and availability requirements. (Action) All at Once: updates all instances simultaneously — fastest, cheapest, but causes brief downtime. Use only in Dev/Test. Rolling: updates instances in batches — no downtime, but mixed versions temporarily serve traffic. Good for non-critical production where slight inconsistency is acceptable. Immutable: creates entirely new instances with new version — old instances untouched. If health checks fail, new instances are terminated and old ones continue. Zero risk to existing users, fastest rollback. Best for critical production workloads. (Result) Implemented All at Once for Dev, Rolling for Staging, and Immutable for Production — each environment has the right balance of speed and safety.

questions.question: A company is migrating from Heroku to AWS and wants the most similar experience. What would you recommend?
questions.answer: (Situation) Team uses Heroku and wants to migrate to AWS without a steep learning curve. (Task) Find an AWS service that mirrors Heroku's PaaS experience. (Action) Recommend AWS Elastic Beanstalk. Like Heroku, Beanstalk abstracts infrastructure management — developers just upload code and the platform handles EC2, load balancing, scaling, and monitoring. The EB CLI offers an 'eb deploy' workflow similar to Heroku's git push. Unlike Heroku, Beanstalk allows full access to the underlying EC2 instances and AWS resources when needed. (Result) Team migrated successfully, reducing infrastructure management overhead while gaining access to the full AWS ecosystem (CloudWatch, RDS, S3) compared to Heroku's more limited add-on marketplace.

questions.question: Your application on Elastic Beanstalk suddenly shows Red health status. Users are reporting the site is down. Walk me through your incident response.
questions.answer: (Situation) Production Beanstalk environment Red — site is down. (Task) Restore service as fast as possible, then diagnose root cause. (Action) Step 1: Check Events tab for the most recent event — often the root cause is immediately visible (e.g., 'Deployment failed', 'EC2 instance terminated'). Step 2: If a recent deployment caused it, trigger a rollback by deploying the previous Application Version from the Application Versions page. Step 3: If the issue is infrastructure (EC2 terminated unexpectedly), check EC2 console for instance status. Step 4: Pull logs from Beanstalk Logs tab to find application-level errors. Step 5: If using Load Balanced environment, check if ELB health checks are passing. (Result) In most cases, deploying the previous version restores service in under 5 minutes while the root cause is investigated separately.

questions.question: A startup expects highly variable traffic — near zero overnight and up to 5,000 concurrent users during business hours. Design their Elastic Beanstalk architecture.
questions.answer: (Situation) Startup with unpredictable traffic needs cost-efficient, scalable architecture. (Task) Design a Beanstalk environment that handles peak load automatically and scales to near-zero overnight. (Action) Use a Load Balanced Elastic Beanstalk environment with Auto Scaling configured as follows: minimum 1 instance (overnight), maximum 10 instances (peak), scale out trigger: CPU > 70% for 5 minutes, scale in trigger: CPU < 30% for 10 minutes. Use Application Load Balancer with health checks. Set a Scheduled Scaling action to pre-warm instances 30 minutes before business hours start. Use instance type t3.medium for the right balance of cost and performance. (Result) Architecture scales automatically — overnight costs approximately $0.04/hr (1 instance), peak costs approximately $0.40/hr (10 instances). No manual intervention required.

questions.question: Compare Elastic Beanstalk with Amazon ECS. When would you choose one over the other?
questions.answer: Elastic Beanstalk is a PaaS optimized for traditional web applications deployed as code archives (ZIP, WAR). It abstracts infrastructure and supports multiple languages natively. It is best for teams that want to deploy quickly without Docker or container expertise. Amazon ECS is a container orchestration service — your application must be packaged as a Docker image. It gives more control over container configuration, task definitions, and service discovery. Choose Beanstalk for: traditional apps, teams new to AWS, fast deployment cycles. Choose ECS for: containerized apps, microservices architectures, teams already using Docker, fine-grained container resource control. Elastic Beanstalk can also run Docker containers, but ECS provides deeper container orchestration capabilities.

questions.question: How would you implement a zero-downtime deployment with instant rollback for a critical Elastic Beanstalk application?
questions.answer: The best approach is Blue/Green deployment using Elastic Beanstalk's environment swap feature. Maintain two environments: Blue (current production, receives all user traffic) and Green (new version, currently idle). Deploy the new version to Green and run all tests. When confident, use Elastic Beanstalk's 'Swap environment URLs' action — this swaps the CNAME DNS entries between the two environments. Users are instantly routed to Green with no downtime. If the new version has issues, swap CNAMEs back to Blue — rollback takes seconds. The key architectural benefit is that rollback is not a re-deploy — it is just a DNS change.

questions.question: How does Elastic Beanstalk handle database lifecycle, and what is the recommended production database architecture?
questions.answer: Elastic Beanstalk can create an RDS database directly within an environment. However, this tightly couples the database lifecycle to the environment — if you terminate the environment, the database is deleted (by default). For production, the recommended architecture is to create RDS independently (outside of Beanstalk), then pass the database connection details to the Beanstalk application via Environment Variables (DB_HOST, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD) or AWS Secrets Manager. This decoupled approach means you can terminate, update, or swap Beanstalk environments without any risk to the database. The database persists independently and can be shared across multiple environments.

questions.question: What are .ebextensions and how would you use them to customize an Elastic Beanstalk environment?
questions.answer: .ebextensions is a directory placed in the root of your application ZIP file. It contains YAML or JSON configuration files (ending in .config) that Elastic Beanstalk processes during deployment. They allow you to: install OS packages (e.g., install git, libpq-dev), run commands or scripts during deployment, create files on the instance, modify Nginx or Apache configuration, configure environment properties, and set AWS resource options. For example, to install a package: create .ebextensions/packages.config containing 'packages: yum: libpq-devel: []'. This is the correct way to customize the environment without SSH-ing into instances manually, which would create configuration drift.

questions.question: A company has a microservices architecture with 8 services. Each service needs independent deployment, scaling, and environments. Is Elastic Beanstalk the right choice? If yes, how would you structure it?
questions.answer: Elastic Beanstalk can work for microservices but has limitations at scale. For 8 services: create one Elastic Beanstalk Application per microservice (8 applications total). Each application has its own Dev, Test, and Production environments. Each environment scales independently. However, at this scale, Amazon ECS (with Docker) or EKS (Kubernetes) becomes more appropriate because: container-based services deploy faster, ECS Service Discovery handles inter-service communication more cleanly, and ECS/EKS has better support for sidecar patterns, health check granularity, and blue/green via CodeDeploy. Recommendation: use Beanstalk if the team lacks Docker expertise and services are traditional web apps. Migrate to ECS/EKS as the architecture matures and container skills develop.
